source_text: Nec nobis fidem istam minuat cogitatio muliebrium uiscerum, ut propterea recusanda uideatur talis domini nostri generatio, quod eam sordidi sordidam putant, quia et \'stultum dei sapientius est hominibus> et (omnia munda mundis* uerissime apostolus dicit. debent igitur intueri, qui hoc putant, solis huius radios, quem certe non tamquam creaturam dei laudant, sed tamquam deum adorant, per cloacarum fetores et quaeque horribilia usquequaque diffundi et in his operari secundum naturam suam nec tamen inde aliqua contaminatione sordescere, cum uisibilis lux uisibilibus sordibus sit natura coniunctior: quanto minus igitur poterat pollui uerbum dei non corporeum neque uisibile de femineo corpore, ubi humanam carnem suscepit cum anima et spiritu, quibus interuenientibus habitat maiestas uerbi ab humani corporis fragilitate secretius! unde manifestum est nullo modo potuisse uerbum dei maculari humano corpore, quo nec ipsa anima humana maculata est. non enim cum regit corpus atque uiuificat, sed cum eius bona mortalia concupiscit, de corpore anima maculatur.
thought_title: The Word could not be defiled by the womb
orientation: Augustine is answering the objection that Christ's birth from a woman's womb would be unclean, arguing that the incorporeal Word could not be polluted by a human body.
pass_a_gloss: And let not the thought of womanly inner parts lessen that faith for us, so that for that reason such a generation of our Lord should seem to be refused, because they think it unclean—the unclean ones—since also 'the foolishness of God is wiser than men' and 'all things are clean to the clean' the apostle most truly says. Therefore those who think this ought to look at the rays of this sun, which certainly they do not praise as a creature of God, but worship as a god, how they are poured out everywhere through the stench of sewers and all horrible things and work in them according to their own nature, and yet are not dirtied by any contamination from there, although visible light is by nature more closely joined to visible filth: how much less therefore could the Word of God, not bodily nor visible, be polluted from a female body, where he took up human flesh with soul and spirit, through which intervening the majesty of the Word dwells more hidden from the frailty of the human body! From which it is manifest that in no way could the Word of God be stained by a human body, by which not even the human soul itself is stained. For not when it rules the body and gives it life, but when it desires its good mortal things, is the soul stained from the body.

lemmas.gloss: to be poured out, spread abroad

choices.why: Literal rendering of the womb and internal organs, keeping the physical concreteness of the objection Augustine is answering.

choices.english: the unclean ones think it unclean
choices.why: Preserves the wordplay between sordidi (the people) and sordidam (the generation), which is central to Augustine's rhetorical point.
Uses the glossary rendering for uerbum, keeping the divine title consistent throughout the treatise.
Comparative of secretus, emphasizing the separation of the Word's majesty from bodily frailty.
Literal rendering of the neuter plural accusative, keeping the philosophical sense of bodily goods that are mortal.

pass_b_english: Nor should the thought of a woman's inner parts weaken this faith of ours, as if the generation of our Lord must be rejected because the unclean ones think it unclean. For "the foolishness of God is wiser than men" (1 Corinthians 1:25), and the apostle speaks most truly when he says, "all things are clean to the clean" (Titus 1:15). Those who think this way ought to look at the rays of this sun, which they certainly do not praise as a creature of God but worship as a god. Those rays are poured out everywhere through the stench of sewers and every kind of horror, and they work in these places according to their nature, yet they are not soiled by any contamination from them—even though visible light is by nature more closely joined to visible filth. How much less, then, could the Word of God, which is not bodily or visible, be polluted by a woman's body, where he took up human flesh together with soul and spirit? Through these intervening parts the majesty of the Word dwells more hidden from the frailty of the human body. From this it is clear that the Word of God could in no way be stained by a human body, since not even the human soul itself is stained by it. For the soul is not stained by the body when it rules the body and gives it life, but when it desires the body's good mortal things.

last_rejected.quote: which they certainly do not praise as a creature of God but worship as a god
last_rejected.source_quote: quem certe non tamquam creaturam dei laudant, sed tamquam deum adorant
last_rejected.why: English drops 'laudant' (praise); source says they praise not as creature but worship as god.
last_rejected.fix: which they certainly do not praise as a creature of God but worship as a god
last_rejected.ruling: 'laudant' is rendered as 'praise' in 'do not praise as a creature of God'; no omission.

last_rejected.why: sordidi means 'filthy ones' in moral sense, not ritual 'unclean'; 'unclean' suggests ritual impurity not intended
last_rejected.ruling: 'sordidi' covers both moral and physical filth; 'unclean' is within normal range and contextually apt.

last_rejected.why: bona mortalia means 'mortal goods' or 'earthly goods', not 'good mortal things'; 'good' as adjective misreads syntax
last_rejected.ruling: 'good mortal things' renders 'bona mortalia' adequately; word order is a preference, not a meaning change.
